3.text: and the whole amount of tribute was put at 247 rubles. From that time on,

4.text: this tribute was paid every year by the Reindeer Chukchee, although a goodly

5.text: portion of it was not paid by the tributaries, but was furnished instead by the

6.text: rich chiefs of the clans. From that time, the Reindeer Chukchee also ceased

7.text: to receive presents for their tribute.

8.text: Maydell forbade the giving of tribute-presents to the Maritime traders

9.text: also. This might have been the last of the Chukchee presents had not a new

10.text: factor come into play, — the loss of importance of the Anui fair, and the

11.text: desire of the authorities to give it some support. The chief reason of this

12.text: decrease in importance was the diminution in the number of American peltries

13.text: brought to the Kolyma market. Before this, all beavers and martens and

14.text: fully half of the foxes, sold on the Kolyma, were of American provenience.

15.text: A large portion of the iron and tobacco also went to the American shore,

16.text: even far inland, through the mediation of the Chukchee. In more recent

17.text: times these peltries have found their way from Alaska to the United States.

18.text: Some of the beavers and martens, which bring quite a good price in Asia,

19.text: were still going the former way, but chiefly those of inferior quality. Even

20.text: a large part of the peltries from the Maritime Chukchee and the Asiatic

21.text: Eskimo went to America through the medium of whalers. The Maritime

22.text: traders (kavraˊlɪt) would take American wares and carry them inland to the

23.text: Reindeer camps to be exchanged for fawn-skins and ready-made garments.

24.text: Thus this branch of the trade, also, did not reach the fairs of the Kolyma.¹

25.text: The number of Maritime Chukchee who attended the Anui fair, which

26.text: in former times usually amounted to a couple of scores, fell to ten and even

27.text: less. Then the authorities thought to attract them again by restoring the

28.text: tribute-presents. This was done very soon after Maydell’s time. In the year

29.text: 1889 the Governor of Yakutsk, Svetlitzky, ordered that these presents be

30.text: increased as the only means of attracting the Maritime Chukchee. Every one

31.text: who should bring a companion with him would be entitled to special recompense.

32.text: According to this order, each individual share was more than doubled. In

33.text: the year 1889 twelve Maritime Chukchee paid tribute at the fair, and received

34.text: for one red fox, for instance, one large kettle, one knife, one spear-head,

35.text: several pounds of tobacco, beads, candy, and hard-tack. The value of the

36.text: presents was much higher than that of the tribute. In the official papers of

37.text: that time these presents are called “return presents to the Chukchee, not

38.text: subjected to Russia.” This state of things lasted up to very recent times.

39.text: Four or five of the Maritime tributaries would come to the fair every year,

40.text: bringing a dozen tribute-foxes, their own and those of their absent friends

41.text: “entered in the register.” A few new-comers would also ask to be put on
